newsitem.title: POLAND: Polish deputies vote to open up communist files.
newsitem.headline: Polish deputies vote to open up communist files.

text.p: The lower house of parliament, heading for a possible clash with President Aleksander Kwasniewski, passed a bill on Friday that would unmask government workers and politicians who spied for Poland's communist-era security police.

The naming of such collaborators could be a burning issue for parliamentary candidates in this year's general election, which will pit parties rooted in the pre-1989 Solidarity opposition against the former communists, in power since 1993.
Unlike some former Soviet bloc countries, Poland has not opened the files of the communist security police.
Supporters of vetting say former agents of the ill-famed SB security service have taken important state jobs and are vulnerable to blackmail.
But others, notably ex-communists, argue it is too late to start exposing former collaborators and the Interior Ministry's archives are too unreliable to carry out a fair vetting.

The draft law was adopted in a 214 votes to 162 vote with 16 abstentions. The Peasant Party, junior partner in the coalition government, joined forces with the right-centrist opposition to out-vote Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz's ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance.
"The vote shows there is a majority in parliament that supports an honest vetting," said Bogdan Pek, head of the parliament committee which drafted the bill.

The ex-communists had tried to water down the bill with a narrow definition of collaboration and a clause protecting former intelligence and counter-intelligence agents. Their amendments were rejected early on Friday, making it more likely that President Kwasniewski, an ex-communist, might veto the bill.
Kwasniewski's aides say the president supports the bill in principle but feels its current form could harm the security services.

"The president has a number of reservations about the bill in its current shape, but the senate may still change the draft law so it is too early to say what he will do with it," presidential spokesman Antoni Styrczula told Reuters.
If the president rejects the bill, the Peasants and opposition are unlikely to muster the two-thirds majority needed to override his veto.
The bill would set up a special vetting court to probe public life for those who were police spies between 1944 and 1990.
People holding or seeking elected posts, senior government positions, judicial and public media jobs would have to openly declare whether they had been informants.

They would face up to five years in prison, stiff fines and a ban from selected state jobs if the court found they had lied. But a declaration that they had collaborated would not in itself automatically block their way to such posts.
Some opposition critics say the legislation does not go far enough because it would unmask low-ranking agents while their masters from the communist party would remain unknown.

They say the bill should give all Poles access to files by setting up an institution, like the Gauck agency in former East Germany, which would oversee unveiling the archives. But most parliamentarians decided this would be too expensive.
